summary: Defines a Capabilities optional parameter for BGP-4 so peers can advertise supported features in the OPEN message. Before this, an unrecognized optional parameter forced a BGP speaker to end peering. It replaces RFC 2842 and was replaced by RFC 5492.

eli5.summary: When two routers meet, they can list what tricks they know. Now an unfamiliar trick no longer ends the conversation, and new features are easier to add.

questions: how do bgp peers negotiate features
what is bgp optional parameter type 2
what is bgp unsupported capability error
subtitle: How two BGP routers tell each other which optional features they support, without breaking the session.

tldr.problem: BGP-4 required a speaker to terminate peering when its OPEN message carried an Optional Parameter it did not recognize, which made adding new features awkward.
tldr.mechanism: A new Optional Parameter, Capabilities (type 2), lets each speaker list the capabilities it supports in its OPEN message as code, length and value triples. A peer that does not understand it answers with a NOTIFICATION and the speaker retries without it.
tldr.outcome: Speakers can now learn what a peer supports and use only those features. This RFC obsoletes RFC 2842 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 5492.

today: RFC 3392 is obsoleted by RFC 5492, which now defines capabilities advertisement with BGP-4. It replaced RFC 2842 when it was published in November 2002.

sections.title: The Problem With Unknown Parameters
sections.content:
BGP-4 sessions start with an OPEN message. Under the base rules, a BGP speaker that receives an OPEN message with one or more unrecognized Optional Parameters must terminate BGP peering. That makes it hard to introduce new capabilities, because any new parameter could cause old peers to drop the session.

RFC 3392 defines a new Optional Parameter called Capabilities. It is expected to make new capabilities easy to introduce by advertising them gracefully, without requiring that BGP peering be terminated.
sections.eli5: Before this, a router that heard a word it did not know would hang up. Now routers can mention extra skills without anyone hanging up.

sections.title: How Capability Advertisement Works
sections.content:
A speaker that supports capabilities advertisement MAY include the Capabilities Optional Parameter in the OPEN message it sends. The parameter lists what the speaker supports. A speaker learns what its peer supports by reading the list in the OPEN message it receives from that peer.

A speaker may use a capability with its peer only after it has determined, in this way, that the peer supports it.

If the peer does not support capabilities advertisement at all, it answers the OPEN with a NOTIFICATION whose Error Subcode is Unsupported Optional Parameter. The speaker SHOULD then try to re-establish the connection without sending the Capabilities parameter.

If a speaker needs a capability that its peer lacks, it MAY send a NOTIFICATION with the Error Subcode Unsupported Capability and end peering. That decision is local to the speaker, and such a peering SHOULD NOT be re-established automatically.
sections.eli5: Each router shows its list of skills. If the other one cannot read lists, they start over without the list. If a skill is truly needed and missing, a router may say goodbye.

sections.title: The Capabilities Optional Parameter
sections.content:
The Capabilities Optional Parameter has Parameter Type 2. It carries one or more triples of Capability Code, Capability Length and Capability Value. The code and length are each one octet. The code identifies the capability, the length gives the size of the value in octets, and the value is variable and interpreted according to the code.

Speakers SHOULD NOT include more than one instance of a capability with the same code, length and value, although extra copies do not change the meaning. A speaker MAY include several instances with the same code and non-zero length but different values. How those are processed is specific to the capability and MUST be described in the document that introduces it.
sections.eli5: Each skill on the list is written as a name tag, a note saying how long the details are, and then the details themselves.

sections.title: The Unsupported Capability Error
sections.content: The RFC adds a new NOTIFICATION Error Subcode, Unsupported Capability, with the value 7. The Data field of the NOTIFICATION SHOULD list the capabilities that caused the speaker to send it, each encoded the same way as in the OPEN message.
sections.eli5: When a router hangs up because a needed skill is missing, it can say which skill was the problem.

sections.title: Capability Code Registry
sections.content:
IANA maintains the registry of Capability Code values. The RFC sets these ranges:

  • 0 is reserved.
  • 1 through 63 are assigned by IANA under the IETF Consensus policy.
  • 64 through 127 are assigned under First Come First Served.
  • 128 through 255 are for Private Use.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of skill numbers. Some numbers need a big group to agree, some go to whoever asks first, and some are free for private use.

sections.title: Security and Changes From RFC 2842
sections.content:
The RFC says this extension does not change the underlying security issues inherent in existing BGP, and points to the TCP MD5 signature option in RFC 2385 as a related protection.

Compared with RFC 2842, the document makes several minor editorial changes and clarifies how to handle multiple instances of the same capability.
sections.eli5: Adding a skill list does not make the routers any safer or less safe than before. The update mostly tidies the wording and explains what to do with repeated entries.
